turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab your obs before the doctor comes in. Uh, my little one was up half the night with a cough, so if I yawn that's why.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh that's rough, umm, no rush. We flicked through those old magazines out there, the crossword was half done already.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ta. Blood pressure one thirty two over seventy eight, pulse seventy six, temp thirty six point eight, sats ninety eight percent, breathing sixteen.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): G'day, I'm Dr Shah. Come through, both of you. Tell me what's been going on, in your own words.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, I woke up and the left side of my face has gone droopy. I stood at the bathroom mirror and the corner of the mouth was hanging down, and I tried to whistle for the dog the way I always do and just air came out, no whistle, and I can't close the left eye, it stays a bit open no matter how hard I try.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She yelled out and I came running. I thought stroke, straight up. My sister had a droopy face a couple of years ago and it settled, but I still got her in the car.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): What a scare. Was it there the second you woke, or did it build after you were up?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Second I opened my eyes, err, so about four hours ago now. I was completely normal at bedtime, I cleaned my teeth and smiled at myself, which sounds vain but that's how I know.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the eye itself, is it watering, or dry and scratchy?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, sort of. It waters, and it feels scratchy if I don't blink on purpose. I've been dabbing it. Not agony, just annoying, and I keep wanting to hold the lid down with a finger.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in an arm or a leg? Any slurring or muddled words?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No arm weakness, I carried the bag from the car. No leg weakness, stairs were fine. Speech is normal, I'm talking heaps, sorry.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise. Headache, dizziness, trouble swallowing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache. Not dizzy. I swallowed tea and toast fine, though I was watching myself in the kettle, which is ridiculous.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Before the face, anything with the ear?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, yesterday arvo the left ear started up, more behind it than deep inside. A niggle, not agony, and it's still dull this morning. I blamed the pillow.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She rubbed it all through dinner. I offered my ibuprofen and she wouldn't take someone else's tablets.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good call. Do you take any regular medicines, and are you allergic to anything, medicines or otherwise?

[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No regular medicines, not even a vitamin, I keep saying I'll start one. No allergies. I had penicillin as a kid for my tonsils and nothing happened, so that's not a problem.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ongoing illnesses, blood pressure, diabetes, anything like that in you?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not me, no, I'm well, touch wood. My father had diabetes in his fifties, on tablets I think. Mum did not, she was sturdy. My younger sister has pressure but no sugar, she's on something for the pressure. My brother is fine, he runs marathons, bit of a show-off.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the ordinary stuff, work, hours, what you eat, exercise, alcohol?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a rates officer at the council, four days a week, about thirty two hours, mostly a desk which makes my shoulders grumpy but that's not why I'm here. Diet is pretty ordinary, lots of veg, I cook most nights, not much takeaway. I walk the dog most mornings, half an hour. Alcohol is a glass of wine with dinner two or three nights, not more. I don't smoke, never have.
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She does walk in any weather. Me, I've got a crook knee, waiting on a scope, so the dog is her job not mine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. Let's look at the face. Eyebrows up, big smile, eyes squeezed shut.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The right eyebrow goes up, the left just sits there, it won't move. Smile is wonky. Left eye won't squeeze, I can still see light.

[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I see it. Left forehead isn't moving, the left eye doesn't fully close, there's a gap, and the smile pulls across to the right. No rash in the ear canal. Arms are strong and equal. Speech is clear.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the light thing bad? I read a thing once about faces and strokes and I've been spiralling since six this morning, I do that, I over-read.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's alright to be frightened. I'll think out loud. The nerve to that side of the face runs in a tight bony canal, and when it swells it gets squeezed, so the muscles go slack, forehead, eye and mouth together. A stroke in the brain usually spares the forehead, so this pattern argues against that. On my list are a facial nerve palsy, Bell's palsy, and less often something deeper. I'm not going to conclude it's a stroke. My leading impression is Bell's palsy. I can't fully rule out a small central cause, but I won't call it that today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Bell's, right. So the nerve is bruised or squeezed, not dead? I want the detail, sorry. Will it come back, and what about the eye in the meantime?
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most folks improve over weeks rather than days. No scan this morning. If it's not clearly settling when I review you, we might organise an MRI, but not today.
[SEG0032] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Mm. She'll google MRI in the car park, just so you know. I'll try to keep that sensible.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's ok. I'll start a steroid to bring the swelling down on the nerve. Prednisalone, fifty milligrams, by mouth, once a day in the morning, for ten days, with food. No taper at that length.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams sounds huge. Will I be starving and awake all night? My sister got puffy on steroids once, that was her, I've never taken them. Chemist today?

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Appetite and sleep can get a bit stirred, that's the usual, keep the course short. Yes, a script for today. For the eye, carmalose drops, one drop in the left eye every two hours while you're awake, and at night tape the lid gently closed so the surface doesn't dry. Don't put some old ointment on it.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Every two hours, tape at night. I'll alarm it, I live by alarms. Can he do the tape? I don't want it stuck to my eyebrow wrong.
[SEG0037] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I can do the tape. I've done dressings, not for her, for my dad years back when he was crook.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Paper tape, not the heavy sticky stuff, and if the skin gets cranky have a break from it. Red eye, pain in the eye itself, or the sight going blurry, that shouldn't wait.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Red, painful, blurry, don't wait. What about work? I've got a rates deadline Thursday and I face people at the counter, this droop is going to be the whole conversation.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Work if you feel up to it, maybe skip the full counter shift for a couple of days, your call. I want to see you back here in a week. If the eye gets red or the sight goes blurry, come back sooner, don't sit on it.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): A week. If the steroid hunger hits, just more veg? And the wine, do I skip it? I don't want to stuff this up.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ease off the wine while you're on the tablets, they can both annoy the stomach. Ordinary meals are fine, no special diet. If sleep is patchy, morning dosing only, never at night.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the script and book the review. My sister's on a steroid for her asthma and she takes hers with yoghurt, but that's her trick, not me prescribing.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yoghurt I can do, I have it anyway. Umm, the ear is still niggling, is that a separate infection or the same nerve? Do I need ear drops?

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same neighbourhood, the nerve runs by the ear, so an ache can tag along. I don't see an ear infection, so no antibiotic drops. Your own paracetamol is fine if you want it, up to a gram four times a day, only if you need it.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Own paracetamol, a gram if I need it, not automatically four times. I think there's a box at home from last winter. I feel less like I'm falling apart, thank you.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Chemist on the way, and I'll watch the lid tonight. Thanks for squeezing us in.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Script, review in a week, sooner if that eye plays up. Go easy this arvo.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): Review is booked, a week from today, morning clinic. Script's here. Take care.

spec.situation: Person woke with one side of the face drooping, cannot close the eye, cannot whistle; no arm weakness, no speech problem, ear pain a day before; doctor examines and starts steroids, eye care explained.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Watery left eye supported, but severity 'mild' is not stated.
bad.text: Watery left eye (category=ophthalmological, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, body_site=left eye, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Scratchy left eye supported, but severity 'mild' is not stated.
bad.text: Scratchy left eye (category=ophthalmological, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, body_site=left eye, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Improvement over weeks and eye protection supported; 'responsible_person=patient' not stated explicitly.
bad.text: Most people improve over weeks; protect the eye while the lid is weak (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: No regular medicines, not even a vitamin.
Patient was completely normal at bedtime before waking with the facial droop.
Left ear pain was more behind the ear than deep inside, described as a niggle/dull ache rather than severe pain.
Eye symptoms were not severe: watering and scratchiness, 'not agony, just annoying'.
Doctor gave red-flag advice to seek earlier review for red eye, pain in the eye itself, or blurred vision; eye pain was omitted from the recorded return precautions.
Examination finding: left eye does not fully close and there is a gap.
Examination finding: arms are strong and equal.
Follow-up was specifically booked for a week from today in the morning clinic.
